title: Classical training of the New Orleans men and the Arban book
summary: He says New Orleans players often had real classical training, citing Kid Thomas and Manuel Perez's markings in the Arban book; Allen asks if all should learn piano.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Learning your horn: teachers, lessons and fees

blocks.x: Yeah, well, I'll just finish it up briefly on chords. These are just, it kind of starts at the beginning. These are the basic things you have before you start thinking about style or anything else. And it would be wonderful for all the musicians to have a complete training in classical music. Real, complete, legitimate training. All the New Orleans, contrary to popular belief, did. From the TOs, and of course this is all rehash of old stuff. But from all the men that you've interviewed and from the guys that I've talked to, they would maybe have two years of ear training before they ever picked their instrument. You mean somebody like Kid Thomas? No, not Kid Thomas. Some of them. But Kid Thomas, he went through the whole Arben book, played it his own way, of course. Can you imagine Arben being like, wah! I didn't know he would do the Arben method. Sure, sure. Went through the Arben method? Yeah, the whole thing from top to bottom. Manuel Mineta showed me the book he used. He's still got it. All the markings, all the Fess's markings and stuff. Yeah. But, and Thomas can, he can read too. He can read better than I can. Because I've seen him do it. Some guy come up with some sheet music on the job with the tip-top clover of specs and want to play some corny thing. And they put the sheet music on it and he read it. I think maybe he was spelling it more than he was reading it, but that's still better than I can do. But I still think that for a bunch of young guys, these are all shortcuts. The New Orleans men, the type of music they played covered a great period of years. Trial and error. Well, like Raymond, for instance. He's the one I can think of offhand because he's almost in the classic New Orleans way of doing things. Getting to a spot and getting stuck and then figuring out his own shortcut from his own sheer genius or intellect, whatever you want to call it. But I was pointing out the basic things. The cornet player, the lead man to learn the melodies, the piano man to learn the right changes, and for the other men, regardless of what instrument they have, to know chords.
Do you think that it would help if every guy took piano in the back?
